tier_reason: Upgraded from D: the peer-reviewed OOPSLA 2022 paper ('A fast in-place interpreter for WebAssembly') has a public artifact (github.com/titzer/oopsla22-artifact: run-execution-experiments.bash, run-translation-experiments.bash, PolyBenchC 4.2.1 sources, engine build commands and the raw data in data-linux-4.15-i7-8700K) comparing Wizard against wasm3, WAMR (classic and fast), JSC, V8 and SpiderMonkey on an i7-8700K. Not A because compiler versions and the PolyBench-to-wasm build flags are not stated, and the paper text itself could not be opened.

corrections.baseline: Rewriting Wasm interpreters wasm3 and WAMR fast-interp (iwasm-fast), plus WAMR classic interpreter and JavaScriptCore's Wasm LLInt (jsc-int); V8 Liftoff/TurboFan and SpiderMonkey tiers also measured (OOPSLA 2022 artifact)
corrections.workload: OOPSLA 2022 artifact: 24 PolyBenchC 4.2.1 kernels compiled to Wasm, run 100 times each on Linux 4.15 / i7-8700K; measures whole-program execution time per engine and per-byte translation (setup) time and translated-code space of each engine's pre-execution step versus Wizard's in-place interpreter (which only builds a side table).
corrections.claimed_speedup: Setup, not throughput: from the artifact's raw data (derived from page data, medians over 24 PolyBench kernels), Wizard's translation step costs about 4.0 ns per Wasm byte versus 23.0 ns for wasm3, 25.9 ns for WAMR fast-interp and 147.7 ns for the JSC LLInt (about 5.8x, 6.5x and 37x faster setup), and its side table is 0.35 bytes per input byte versus 2.42 (wasm3) and 3.8 (WAMR fast). Execution time (geomean, derived from page data): about 2.5x slower than wasm3, 1.55x slower than WAMR fast-interp, about 1.1x faster than WAMR classic, and on par with jsc-int. Artifact README states: translation time for Wizard 3-4 ns/byte versus ~20-200 ns/byte for rewriting interpreters; Wizard within 1.5x-3.5x of wasm3, on par with wamr-classic (+/-10%) and jsc-int (+/-5%). README: hand-written x86-64 interpreter 'nearly 40x faster than the simple interpreter' (internal baseline).
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-8700K, Linux 4.15 (data-linux-4.15-i7-8700K); a second data set on Ryzen 9 5950X / Linux 5.13 is in the artifact
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Engines built per artifact src/README.md: V8 gn args is_debug=false; JSC build-jsc --jsc-only; wasm3 and WAMR plain cmake (default build type is Release in current CMakeLists); Wizard via the Virgil (aeneas) bootstrap and make bin/wizeng.x86-64-linux on branch exp_fast_config. Compiler versions and PolyBench-to-wasm flags not stated.
corrections.caveats: The win is setup time and memory, not raw speed: in the paper's own data Wizard's in-place interpreter runs about 2.5x slower than wasm3 and 1.55x slower than WAMR fast-interp (geomean over 24 PolyBenchC kernels), beats only WAMR classic (about 1.1x) and ties the JSC LLInt. Numbers are from the 2022 paper build (branch exp_fast_config, source zips on Google Drive) and the wasm3/WAMR-fast binaries were instrumented branches; current Wizard (Wasm 3.0, SPC compiler) is unmeasured. The fast interpreter exists only on x86-64-linux. Wizard is written in Virgil and ships as a standalone engine binary, not a C/C++ library. The paper PDF (arXiv 2205.01183, ACM, Tufts copy) was blocked here; claims come from the artifact README and raw data files.

notes: Found the paper's artifact repo (titzer/oopsla22-artifact) and recomputed ratios from data-linux-4.15-i7-8700K: Wizard setup is about 6x cheaper than wasm3/WAMR-fast and 37x cheaper than JSC LLInt, but execution is slower than wasm3 and WAMR-fast. The record's metric should be startup (translation time) rather than throughput; shortcoming to record: not faster at execution than the fastest interpreters, Virgil engine not a C++ library, numbers from 2022 code.

tier_reason: First-party README table (CPython 3.7 11.787 s, Nuitka 10.039 s, PyPy 1.78 s, prometeo 0.657 s) with the CPU model stated and the benchmark source in examples/fibonacci/fibonacci.py, but the Python-side timing harness, interpreter versions and the C compiler and flags behind the table are not stated, so C, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Fibonacci CPU time (README and examples/fibonacci/CPU_time.txt): CPython 3.7 11.787 s, Nuitka 10.039 s, PyPy3.7 1.78 s, prometeo 0.657 s, about 17.9x faster than CPython, 15.3x faster than Nuitka and 2.7x faster than PyPy (derived from page data). An earlier run set in CPU_time.txt reads Python 27.128 s, Nuitka 12.525 s, prometeo 0.6999 s. Riccati factorization (benchmarks/riccati_benchmark_*.json, derived from page data): prometeo 2.1x-35.7x faster than NumPy and 2.0x-18.3x faster than Julia across sizes, and 0.84x-1.04x of hand-written C with BLASFEO (parity).
corrections.workload: Fibonacci: examples/fibonacci/fibonacci.py computes an iterative fib(n) (integer loop, not recursion) 1,000,000 times for each n from 0 to 29 (3e7 calls), run under CPython, Nuitka, PyPy and as prometeo-generated C. Riccati: examples riccati_mass_spring benchmark over state sizes 4-292 versus hand-written BLASFEO C, NumPy and Julia (benchmarks/run_benchmark*.py).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Generated C is built by pmt's Makefile template with gcc -fPIC -std=c99 and no optimization flag (current template; not stated as the build behind the README table). Python-side harness and flags not in the repo.
corrections.caveats: The Fibonacci source is in the repo (examples/fibonacci/fibonacci.py with raw times in CPU_time.txt), but how CPython, Nuitka and PyPy were timed is not, and their versions are only partly given (Python 3.7, PyPy3.7). CPU_time.txt labels the run '10E7 runs' while the code makes 3e7 calls. The benchmark is a statically typed integer loop compiled to C, so an 18x win over CPython says little about general Python code; prometeo accepts only a typed Python subset. The current Makefile template compiles generated C without -O, so the C path may be unoptimized. Not an interpreter: a Python-subset-to-C transpiler compared with CPython, filed here as the closest category. Last commit 2022-05-19.

notes: Numbers match the README; the record wrongly said the Fibonacci source was missing (it is at examples/fibonacci/) and called it recursion (it is an iterative loop). Riccati data files exist and give derived ratios versus NumPy and Julia. Shortcoming to record: toy integer benchmark, Python-side harness missing, transpiler of a typed subset rather than an interpreter, abandoned since 2022.
